sections.6:
Bosak registers one- and two-argument forms of both functions. Empty input returns
an empty sequence. Untyped atomic values are converted to doubles; explicitly
supplied strings remain strings. Thus untyped XML numbers `2` and `10` have a
numeric range, while string values `'2'` and `'10'` have a lexical range.
Numeric NaN contaminates either extreme; the application must screen it when
missing measurements should be excluded. Mixing number and string raises
`FORG0006` in these fixtures.

QNames are ordered by namespace URI and then local name in codepoint order.
Prefixes do not determine ordering. Equivalent QNames may carry different
prefixes, so the report prints expanded names rather than asserting a chosen
prefix. The draft leaves the chosen representative of equal extrema unspecified.

The second argument selects string collation. Bosak accepts the demonstrated
empty-collation form in both profiles; only the 4.0 draft's default-on-empty
contract is claimed. Keyword `values` matches the reviewed parameter name and
requires 4.0 syntax.

**Observed contract gaps:** mixed numeric values are still promoted in Bosak.
`min((3.1, 3.1e0))` produces a double whose exact comparison with decimal `3.1`
is `1`; under the pinned draft's ordering the minimum is the decimal and that
comparison should be `0`. The equal-highest integer/float example produces a
double even though that converted input value is not the selected extreme.
The integer/decimal probe also returns a decimal rather than preserving the
winning integer. Plain durations remain refused with `FORG0006`, although the
reviewed atomic comparator defines their ordering. Fixtures marked `observed`
record these limits; they are not conforming-result assertions.
When an engine correction lands, update those observed expectations and retain
the historical behavior and migration note alongside the corrected contract.

sections.13:
Complete synthetic input:

```xml
<batch xmlns:q="urn:qa:codes" xmlns:e="urn:erp:codes"><reading id="A" value="2.5" code="q:low"/><reading id="B" value="7.5" code="q:high"/><reading id="C" value="5" code="e:normal"/><reading id="D" value="invalid" code="q:invalid"/><reading id="E" value="" code="q:missing"/></batch>
```

### XPath 4.0 report

[Runnable file](../examples/batch-extrema/main.xpath):

```xpath
let $rows := parse-xml('<batch xmlns:q="urn:qa:codes" xmlns:e="urn:erp:codes"><reading id="A" value="2.5" code="q:low"/><reading id="B" value="7.5" code="q:high"/><reading id="C" value="5" code="e:normal"/><reading id="D" value="invalid" code="q:invalid"/><reading id="E" value="" code="q:missing"/></batch>')/batch/reading
return let $valid := $rows[@value castable as xs:decimal]
return let $invalid := $rows[not(@value castable as xs:decimal)]
return let $values := $valid/@value ! xs:decimal(.)
return let $codes := $rows ! resolve-QName(string(@code), .)
return let $label := function($q) { if (empty($q)) then '-' else concat('Q{', namespace-uri-from-QName($q), '}', local-name-from-QName($q)) }
return let $first := min($codes)
return let $last := max($codes)
return let $low := min($values)
return let $high := max($values)
return concat('accepted=', string-join($valid/@id, ','), '; rejected=', string-join($invalid/@id, ','), '; min=', if (empty($low)) then '-' else string($low), '; max=', if (empty($high)) then '-' else string($high), '; first-code=', $label($first), '; last-code=', $label($last))
```

Exact output:

```text
accepted=A,B,C; rejected=D,E; min=2.5; max=7.5; first-code=Q{urn:erp:codes}normal; last-code=Q{urn:qa:codes}missing
```

A, B and C supply valid decimals; D and E remain rejected identifiers. The ERP
namespace sorts before the QA namespace; within QA, `missing` is the last local
name. This explains the code endpoints without assigning a business rank.

### XPath 3.1 comparison

[Runnable file](../examples/batch-extrema/baseline.xpath):

```xpath
let $rows := parse-xml('<batch xmlns:q="urn:qa:codes" xmlns:e="urn:erp:codes"><reading id="A" value="2.5" code="q:low"/><reading id="B" value="7.5" code="q:high"/><reading id="C" value="5" code="e:normal"/><reading id="D" value="invalid" code="q:invalid"/><reading id="E" value="" code="q:missing"/></batch>')/batch/reading
return let $valid := $rows[@value castable as xs:decimal]
return let $invalid := $rows[not(@value castable as xs:decimal)]
return let $values := $valid/@value ! xs:decimal(.)
return let $codes := $rows ! resolve-QName(string(@code), .)
return let $label := function($q) { if (empty($q)) then '-' else concat('Q{', namespace-uri-from-QName($q), '}', local-name-from-QName($q)) }
return let $cp := 'http://www.w3.org/2005/xpath-functions/collation/codepoint'
return let $less := function($a, $b) {
  let $ns := compare(namespace-uri-from-QName($a), namespace-uri-from-QName($b), $cp)
  return if ($ns eq 0) then compare(local-name-from-QName($a), local-name-from-QName($b), $cp) lt 0 else $ns lt 0
}
return let $first := fold-left($codes, (), function($best, $next) { if (empty($best)) then $next else if ($less($next, $best)) then $next else $best })
return let $last := fold-left($codes, (), function($best, $next) { if (empty($best)) then $next else if ($less($best, $next)) then $next else $best })
return let $low := min($values)
return let $high := max($values)
return concat('accepted=', string-join($valid/@id, ','), '; rejected=', string-join($invalid/@id, ','), '; min=', if (empty($low)) then '-' else string($low), '; max=', if (empty($high)) then '-' else string($high), '; first-code=', $label($first), '; last-code=', $label($last))
```

Exact output:

```text
accepted=A,B,C; rejected=D,E; min=2.5; max=7.5; first-code=Q{urn:erp:codes}normal; last-code=Q{urn:qa:codes}missing
```

The fold comparator performs two comparisons, preserving the namespace/local-name
ordering even when one namespace URI is a prefix of another. The numeric part
uses the same explicit decimal normalization policy as the 4.0 report.

sections.6:
`while-do($input, $predicate, $action)` tests the current value before updating
it. False or empty returns that value immediately; true calls the action and
repeats with the new value. Position starts at one and increments after an action.

`do-until($input, $action, $predicate)` always calls the action first, then tests
its new value using the same position. True returns it; false or empty repeats
at the next position. Note the opposite meanings of a true predicate and the
opposite callback argument order.

Both callbacks receive the **whole current `item()*` value**, not individual
members of a sequence. Actions may return any sequence, including empty.
Predicates return `xs:boolean?`; a status string is not a boolean and raises
XPTY0004. Callback arguments must be callable. The examples use two-argument
inline functions to show both state and position explicitly.
sections.11:
A finite budget plus an action that increments attempts guarantees termination
for these fixtures, even if no response ever reports acceptance. The loops have
no implicit maximum iteration count or delay. An unchanged state with a predicate
that never stops could run indefinitely; every runnable case here has a bound
or a predicate that terminates on its first call. Exceptions propagate; the
functions do not automatically convert them into retryable outcomes.

sections.13:
Complete synthetic input: a gateway status-check sequence for invoice INV-2048.
The third response remains unread because the second response is accepted.

```xml
<submission id="INV-2048">
  <response status="pending"/>
  <response status="accepted"/>
  <response status="pending"/>
</submission>
```

### Test before the action

[Runnable while-do expression](../examples/bounded-retries/while-main.xpath):

```xpath
let $responses := parse-xml('<submission id="INV-2048"><response status="pending"/><response status="accepted"/><response status="pending"/></submission>')/submission/response
let $limit := 3
let $initial := map {'attempts': 0, 'status': 'pending', 'trace': ()}
let $advance := function($state, $position) {
  let $status := string(($responses[$position]/@status, 'pending')[1])
  return map {'attempts': $state?attempts + 1,
              'status': $status,
              'trace': ($state?trace, $status)}
}
let $final := while-do($initial, function($state, $position) { $state?status ne 'accepted' and $state?attempts lt $limit }, $advance)
```

sections.6:
`partial-apply($function, $arguments)` takes a callable and a map with positive
integer keys identifying **one-based** argument positions. Unbound parameters
retain their original relative order. Binding all parameters gives arity zero;
an empty map returns the original callable. Keys beyond the function's arity
are ignored, rather than reporting a misspelled configuration position.
String, zero and negative keys raise XPTY0004 in the demonstrated cases.
Maps and arrays are callable too, and can have their single lookup argument bound.

Supplied values undergo function conversion when parameter metadata permits.
Some Bosak built-ins lack that metadata; their conversion errors may surface
when the resulting function is invoked. The bound-type-error fixture exercises
that call, rather than claiming all validation happens eagerly.

`identity($input)` returns the same `item()*` value, including an empty sequence,
a whole sequence or a container. For nodes it preserves identity, rather than
copying. `identity#1` supplies a function item where a callback is required.

sections.6:
`trim-space` removes XML whitespace (space, tab, CR and LF) at the selected start/end/both boundary. It preserves interior whitespace and does not remove NBSP. Empty input returns an empty string. `pad-string` defaults to end padding with spaces; options select side and padding. It never truncates. Both-side odd padding puts the extra character at the end.

`characters` returns one string per Unicode codepoint; `graphemes` groups supported combining/ZWJ sequences into clusters. Neither performs Unicode normalization. `char` constructs a string from a positive codepoint, recognized entity name or supported escape; some entity names return multiple codepoints. It is not an HTML document decoder.

Bosak's [Graphemes_1/GraphemeClusterClass implementation](../../../src/Bosak.XPath.Standard/Functions/FunctionLibrary.cs) approximates segmentation: it does not distinguish Hangul jamo, Prepend, regional-indicator or full Indic/extended-pictographic classes. Complete synthetic input; the name contains e followed by combining acute, two interior spaces and a truck emoji:

### Complete XPath 4.0 expression

[Runnable file](../examples/customer-text-cleanup/main.xpath):

```xpath
let $name := string(parse-xml('<customer><name>  José  🚚  </name></customer>')/customer/name)
```

sections.6:
`parse-uri` returns an optional map with raw and derived fields, including scheme,
host, integer port, path, decoded path-segments, query, decoded query-parameters
and fragment. Repeated query keys collect a sequence of values. Parsing query
parameters applies form decoding: plus becomes space before percent decoding.
An encoded `%2B` becomes a literal plus. Empty input returns empty.

`build-uri` takes a component map. Nonempty path-segments take precedence over
path in the demonstrated cases; a nonempty query-parameters map takes precedence
over query. A leading empty segment supplies the initial slash. Each hierarchical
segment is encoded independently, so a slash inside a segment becomes `%2F`.
Query values use their own delimiter-encoding rules. Non-hierarchical schemes
such as mailto have different assembly rules; this entry's business route is HTTPS.

`decode-from-uri` percent-decodes UTF-8 and leaves ordinary plus signs unchanged.
Empty input becomes a zero-length string, unlike parse-uri's empty result.
Malformed escapes, invalid UTF-8 and XML-invalid characters become U+FFFD
replacement characters in the specified cases, rather than throwing a strict
validation error. Do not decode the entire address before identifying its boundaries.

The functions have optional options maps for parsing/building. This case uses
`omit-default-ports` to omit HTTPS port 443; a nondefault port is preserved.
The entry verifies that option and default behavior, not every option/signature.

Bosak registers `compare#2` and `compare#3`. The result is `-1`, `0` or `1`, or an
empty sequence if either comparand is absent. Two numeric values use 4.0 atomic
ordering; unrelated type families such as number and string raise `XPTY0004`.

The third argument selects string collation. The 4.0 empty-collation form uses the

```xpath
    if ($row/@kind = 'float') then xs:float($row/@value) else xs:double($row/@value)
  return let $limit := xs:decimal($row/@limit)
  return let $status := if (empty($value) or not($value eq $value)) then 'missing' else
    let $order := compare($value, $limit)
    return if ($order lt 0) then 'below' else if ($order eq 0) then 'at-limit' else 'above'
  return concat($row/@id, '=', $status), ';')
```

```text
A=at-limit;B=above;C=below;D=missing;E=missing
```

their distinct binary representations. D contains numeric NaN and E has no value;
both are reported as missing instead of being silently ranked below the limit.

### XPath 3.1 comparison with explicit normalization

[Runnable file](../examples/measurement-comparison/baseline.xpath):

```xpath

return string-join(for $row in $rows return
  let $value := if (string($row/@value) = '') then () else
    if ($row/@kind = 'decimal') then xs:decimal($row/@value) else
    if ($row/@kind = 'float') then xs:float($row/@value) else xs:double($row/@value)
  return let $limit := xs:decimal($row/@limit)
  return let $status := if (empty($value) or not($value eq $value)) then 'missing' else
    let $normalized := xs:double($value)
    return let $boundary := xs:double($limit)
    return if ($normalized lt $boundary) then 'below' else if ($normalized eq $boundary) then 'at-limit' else 'above'
  return concat($row/@id, '=', $status), ';')
```

```text

```

sections.6:
`days-in-month` accepts an optional `xs:dateTime`, `xs:date` or `xs:gYearMonth`,
returning 28, 29, 30 or 31 for its **local** year/month. A value whose UTC instant
falls in February may still have a March local month. Leap years are divisible
by four, except centuries not divisible by 400. Empty input returns empty.

`build-dateTime` constructs a Gregorian value from a component map. Full date
and clock components plus timezone produce `xs:dateTimeStamp`; omitting timezone
produces `xs:dateTime` without inventing an offset. Date-only fields produce
`xs:date`, and clock-only fields produce `xs:time`. Empty input returns empty.
Unused components can be absent or empty; arbitrary incomplete field combinations
raise FODT0005. Invalid calendar/clock values raise FORG0001; an offset outside
±14 hours raises FODT0003. Midnight uses hour zero, not 24.

sections.6: XPath uses one-based positions and inclusive slice ends. Empty/zero bounds mean defaults, not JavaScript’s zero-based origin. Negative bounds count from the end. sections.11: Out-of-range `items-at` positions are ignored; duplicate requested positions remain duplicated. A separator can contain several items, and no separator is inserted for empty or singleton input. Negative-step slices reverse traversal, while a mismatched explicit direction yields no items.

sections.6:
Both functions accept an `item()*` input and a predicate receiving the item and
its one-based input position, returning `xs:boolean?`. `false()` or `()` marks
the boundary. `take-while` excludes that item; `drop-while` includes it and all
later items. Empty input gives empty results; all matching input is returned by
`take-while` and removed by `drop-while`. A string such as `'ready'` is not a
boolean predicate result and raises XPTY0004. Bosak also accepts a map as a
one-argument callable predicate; a missing key returns empty and stops selection.
The fixtures use ordinary two-argument inline functions for the business rule.
sections.11:
The first held order and every later ready order remain visible. No order is
silently discarded or moved. An empty queue needs no dispatch; an entirely ready
queue leaves no remainder. These are selection decisions, not operational side effects.

sections.13:
The synthetic fixture represents a warehouse queue in arrival order. ORD103 is
held for investigation; ORD104 must wait behind it despite its ready status.

```xml
<queue>
  <order id="ORD101" status="ready"/>
  <order id="ORD102" status="ready"/>
  <order id="ORD103" status="hold"/>
  <order id="ORD104" status="ready"/>
</queue>
```

Complete XPath 4.0 expression ([runnable file](../examples/ordered-queue-prefix/main.xpath)):

```xpath
let $queue := parse-xml('<queue><order id="ORD101" status="ready"/><order id="ORD102" status="ready"/><order id="ORD103" status="hold"/><order id="ORD104" status="ready"/></queue>')/queue/order
let $ready := function($order, $position) { string($order/@status) eq 'ready' }
let $dispatch := take-while($queue, $ready)
let $retained := drop-while($queue, $ready)
return concat('dispatch=', string-join($dispatch/@id, ','), '; retained=', string-join($retained/@id, ','))
```

Exact output:

```text
dispatch=ORD101,ORD102; retained=ORD103,ORD104
```

Complete XPath 3.1 comparison ([runnable file](../examples/ordered-queue-prefix/baseline.xpath)):

```xpath
let $queue := parse-xml('<queue><order id="ORD101" status="ready"/><order id="ORD102" status="ready"/><order id="ORD103" status="hold"/><order id="ORD104" status="ready"/></queue>')/queue/order
return let $stop := ((for $i in 1 to count($queue) return if (string($queue[$i]/@status) eq 'ready') then () else $i)[1], count($queue) + 1)[1]
return let $dispatch := subsequence($queue, 1, $stop - 1)
return let $retained := subsequence($queue, $stop)
return concat('dispatch=', string-join($dispatch/@id, ','), '; retained=', string-join($retained/@id, ','))
```

Its exact output is identical. A whole-queue filter instead returns
`ORD101,ORD102,ORD104`, as the [filter comparison](../examples/ordered-queue-prefix/filter-comparison.xpath)
verifies. It would allow ORD104 to overtake the held order.

sections.6:
The signature takes a `node()?` start and a step callback returning `node()*`.
It finds nodes reachable in **one or more steps**, removes duplicates by node
identity, and delivers the result in document order. Empty start returns empty.
The start is absent unless a step path reaches it again; cycles can therefore
put the start in the result. Use node union to include it unconditionally.
Non-node input, multiple start nodes or non-node step results raise XPTY0004.

The pinned evolving specification also discusses JNodes. This entry verifies
XML nodes in one document and does not assert JSON-node or cross-document
ordering support. Node identity differs from equality of `@id` strings.

include KIT itself. The result does not preserve dependency-path order and cannot
be used directly as an installation sequence. It also does not compute quantities:
several paths to BOLT still produce one BOLT node. Quantity explosion requires
separate path/multiplicity rules.

Full synthetic catalog input. BOLT is deliberately placed before its referring
components to make document order visibly different from traversal order.

```xml
<catalog>
  <part id="KIT"><needs ref="FRAME"/><needs ref="MOTOR"/></part>
  <part id="BOLT"/>
```

[Complete XPath 4.0 expression](../examples/product-dependency-closure/main.xpath):

```xpath

let $start := $parts[@id eq 'KIT']
let $step := function($part) { $parts[@id = $part/needs/@ref] }
let $reachable := transitive-closure($start, $step)
return concat('dependencies=', string-join($reachable/@id, ','), '; count=', count($reachable))
```

```xpath
return let $start := $parts[@id eq 'KIT']
return let $step := function($part) { $parts[@id = $part/needs/@ref] }
return let $reachable := fold-left(1 to count($parts), $step($start) | (), function($seen, $round) { $seen | ($seen ! $step(.)) })
return concat('dependencies=', string-join($reachable/@id, ','), '; count=', count($reachable))
```

```text
dependencies=BOLT,FRAME,MOTOR; count=3
```

sections.6:
Matching uses adjacent sequence positions, preserving order and repeated
events. The mathematical term subsequence can allow gaps; these functions
require a contiguous segment, prefix or suffix. Default item comparison is
`deep-equal`, so maps are compared by content, including unrelated fields.
The custom record comparator intentionally projects only the state code.

Comparators receive `(input-item, required-item)` and must have arity two. Their
direction is observable when the callback is asymmetric. A boolean or empty
sequence is returned: empty means false, while the string `'yes'` fails
XPTY0004 rather than being treated as a truthy JavaScript value.
`all-equal` follows atomized `distinct-values` semantics, including collation,
numeric comparison and NaN grouping, rather than comparing every item to the
first with general `=`.
sections.11:
Empty required sequences match any input, including empty input. A nonempty
requirement longer than the input fails. `all-equal` is true for empty and
singleton values; the report separately requires events and one identity per
event. Path selection of missing identities/codes drops values, so count guards
are deliberate. The empty-history example also explains vacuous `known=true`.

Callback selection can change business meaning: the record example ignores
timestamps and normalizes code casing while the default compares full maps.
The supplied ASCII case-insensitive collation treats SHIP-42 and ship-42 as equal;
the default codepoint comparison keeps them distinct. Use that collation only
when the identifier contract permits it. NaN grouping is an equality contract,
not evidence that invalid measurement values are acceptable.

sections.13:
The synthetic carrier vocabulary below has one shipment header and ordered
event records. Each event supplies its shipment identity and state code. The
fixtures use document order as event order; production feeds must establish that
ordering before applying the checks. No timestamps, carrier standard, resource
access or application variables are assumed.

**Normal input:**

```xml
<history shipment="SHIP-42">
  <event shipment="SHIP-42" code="CREATED"/>
  <event shipment="SHIP-42" code="PICKED"/>
  <event shipment="SHIP-42" code="PACKED"/>
  <event shipment="SHIP-42" code="DISPATCHED"/>
  <event shipment="SHIP-42" code="IN_TRANSIT"/>
  <event shipment="SHIP-42" code="DELIVERED"/>
</history>
```

| Report field | Business check |
|---|---|
| `shipment`, `events` | Header identity and observed event count. |
| `consistent` | There is at least one event, every event has an identity, and all identities agree with the header. |
| `known` | Every event has a code and each code belongs to the declared vocabulary. |
| `start` | The first two events are CREATED then PICKED. |
| `dispatch` | PACKED immediately precedes DISPATCHED somewhere in the history. |
| `end` | DELIVERED is the final event. |
| `ready` | All five checks hold. This report flag is the demo's acceptance decision. |

**Complete XPath40 report — mode 40:** [main.xpath](../examples/shipment-event-sequences/main.xpath)

```xquery
(: Synthetic carrier history; document order is the agreed event order. :)
let $history := parse-xml('<history shipment="SHIP-42"><event shipment="SHIP-42" code="CREATED"/><event shipment="SHIP-42" code="PICKED"/><event shipment="SHIP-42" code="PACKED"/><event shipment="SHIP-42" code="DISPATCHED"/><event shipment="SHIP-42" code="IN_TRANSIT"/><event shipment="SHIP-42" code="DELIVERED"/></history>')/history,
    $events := $history/event,
    $codes := $events/@code ! string(.),
    $ids := $events/@shipment ! string(.),
    $consistent := exists($events) and count($ids) eq count($events)
                   and (all-equal($ids)) and $ids[1] eq string($history/@shipment),
    $known := count($codes) eq count($events) and
              (every $code in $codes satisfies $code = ('CREATED','PICKED','PACKED','DISPATCHED','IN_TRANSIT','DELIVERED')),
    $start := starts-with-subsequence($codes,('CREATED','PICKED')),
    $dispatch := contains-subsequence($codes,('PACKED','DISPATCHED')),
    $end := ends-with-subsequence($codes,('DELIVERED'))
return concat('shipment=', $history/@shipment, ';events=', count($events),
              ';consistent=', $consistent, ';known=', $known, ';start=', $start,
              ';dispatch=', $dispatch, ';end=', $end,
              ';ready=', $consistent and $known and $start and $dispatch and $end)
```

Exact output:

```text
shipment=SHIP-42;events=6;consistent=true;known=true;start=true;dispatch=true;end=true;ready=true
```

**XPath31 comparison — mode 31:** [baseline.xpath](../examples/shipment-event-sequences/baseline.xpath)

```xquery
(: Synthetic carrier history; document order is the agreed event order. :)
let $history := parse-xml('<history shipment="SHIP-42"><event shipment="SHIP-42" code="CREATED"/><event shipment="SHIP-42" code="PICKED"/><event shipment="SHIP-42" code="PACKED"/><event shipment="SHIP-42" code="DISPATCHED"/><event shipment="SHIP-42" code="IN_TRANSIT"/><event shipment="SHIP-42" code="DELIVERED"/></history>')/history,
    $events := $history/event,
    $codes := $events/@code ! string(.),
    $ids := $events/@shipment ! string(.),
    $consistent := exists($events) and count($ids) eq count($events)
                   and (count(distinct-values($ids)) le 1) and $ids[1] eq string($history/@shipment),
    $known := count($codes) eq count($events) and
              (every $code in $codes satisfies $code = ('CREATED','PICKED','PACKED','DISPATCHED','IN_TRANSIT','DELIVERED')),
    $start := deep-equal(subsequence($codes,1,2),('CREATED','PICKED')),
    $dispatch := some $i in 1 to (count($codes)-1) satisfies deep-equal(subsequence($codes,$i,2),('PACKED','DISPATCHED')),
    $end := deep-equal(subsequence($codes,count($codes),1),('DELIVERED'))
return concat('shipment=', $history/@shipment, ';events=', count($events),
              ';consistent=', $consistent, ';known=', $known, ';start=', $start,
              ';dispatch=', $dispatch, ';end=', $end,
              ';ready=', $consistent and $known and $start and $dispatch and $end)
```

Complete synthetic input:

```xml
<offers><offer id="A" price="10" score="90"/><offer id="B" price="8" score="90"/><offer id="C" price="8" score="85"/><offer id="D" price="12" score="92"/></offers>
```

### XPath 4.0 expression

[Runnable file](../examples/supplier-offer-ranking/main.xpath):

```xpath
let $offers := parse-xml('<offers><offer id="A" price="10" score="90"/><offer id="B" price="8" score="90"/><offer id="C" price="8" score="85"/><offer id="D" price="12" score="92"/></offers>')/offers/offer
let $price := function($o) { xs:decimal($o/@price) }
let $score := function($o) { xs:decimal($o/@score) }
let $boundary := lowest($offers, (), $price)
let $cheapest := if (empty($boundary)) then () else $offers[$price(.) eq $price($boundary[1])]
let $collation := 'http://www.w3.org/2005/xpath-functions/collation/codepoint'
return concat('cheapest=', string-join($cheapest/@id, ','), '; bestScore=', string-join(highest($offers, (), $score)/@id, ','), '; ranked=', string-join(sort-by($offers, (map {'key': $price}, map {'key': $score, 'order': 'descending'})) ! string(@id), ','), '; collationAvailable=', collation-available($collation))
```

Exact output:

```text
cheapest=B,C; bestScore=D; ranked=B,C,A,D; collationAvailable=true
```

### XPath 3.1 comparison

[Runnable file](../examples/supplier-offer-ranking/baseline.xpath):

```xpath
let $offers := parse-xml('<offers><offer id="A" price="10" score="90"/><offer id="B" price="8" score="90"/><offer id="C" price="8" score="85"/><offer id="D" price="12" score="92"/></offers>')/offers/offer
return let $cheap := min($offers/@price ! xs:decimal(.))
return let $best := max($offers/@score ! xs:decimal(.))
return let $byScore := sort($offers, (), function($o) { -xs:decimal($o/@score) })
return let $ranked := sort($byScore, (), function($o) { xs:decimal($o/@price) })
return concat('cheapest=', string-join($offers[xs:decimal(@price) eq $cheap]/@id, ','), '; bestScore=', string-join($offers[xs:decimal(@score) eq $best]/@id, ','), '; ranked=', string-join($ranked ! string(@id), ','))
```

sections.6:
`unix-dateTime` uses **nonnegative epoch milliseconds**, returning a UTC
`xs:dateTimeStamp` in Bosak. Omitted or empty input means zero (the epoch),
not the current time. A negative argument raises FOCA0002. Unix time assumes
86,400-second days and does not account for leap seconds.

`seconds` accepts an optional decimal count, returning a day-time duration with
fractional and negative values preserved. `duration-to-seconds` returns an
optional decimal total for a day-time duration. Both return empty for empty input.
For example PT1M30S has total 90 seconds but a seconds component of 30.
Year-month durations cannot be converted to a fixed seconds count by this rule.
sections.11:
Fractional measurements survive the conversion. A negative remaining duration
signals lateness without losing its magnitude. None of these functions sleeps,
retries a request, cancels processing or checks the current wall clock.
Calling `unix-dateTime()` always returns the epoch, which must not be mistaken
for a receipt's missing timestamp.

Structured userinfo/host/port take precedence over raw authority when any is present. sections.6:
Both functions have one-, two- and three-argument forms. Omitted/empty collation
uses the context default. An omitted key uses atomized input values. Explicit
empty keys currently raise `XPTY0004` in the nonempty sequence/array probes,
although the reviewed 4.0 draft defines default-on-empty. Supply `data#1`
explicitly as a verified workaround; an empty key argument differs from a key
callback that returns an empty sequence. A key can be a sequence: values are compared lexicographically,
with the first differing position determining order. Equal complete keys preserve
input order; an empty key precedes a nonempty key.

The sequence callback receives one input item. The array callback receives a
whole member, which can contain multiple items or be empty. Sorting rearranges
members without flattening their payload. `array:append` deliberately creates
one two-item member per line; an `array { ... }` constructor over a flat sequence
would create different member boundaries.

**Observed numeric gaps:** Bosak's retained functions use the shared
`XdmValueComparer`, rather than the reviewed exact numeric ordering. Input
`(3.1e0, 3.1)` remains double then decimal because promotion makes its keys tie;
the reviewed 4.0 ordering puts decimal first. Both sequence and array probes
record that limit. The two-item NaN probes also depend on input direction:
`(NaN, 1)` produces number then NaN, while `(1, NaN)` produces NaN then number.
The pinned numeric ordering places NaN below numbers. These are observed gaps,
not a promised ordering policy for larger inputs. Corrected engine behavior must
update the observed expectations while retaining historical migration notes.

QName keys are refused in the demonstrated case. The reviewed sorting rules also
exclude nonordered QName keys; broader `fn:compare` support does not authorize
assuming every atomic family is a valid sort key. Bosak accepts the unknown-collation URI in both empty-input and nonempty-string
probes; the latter returns codepoint-like order rather than `FOCH0002`. These
results do not establish that the URI is supported. Use a known explicit
collation and keep unknown-URI validation as an implementation follow-up.
